numberHierarchy.title: Number Hierarchy

hints.build: click a point or a row name, or play to fill the rows from the bottom
hints.disguised: click a number, or play to check them one by one

intro.build: every row holds all the points of the rows below it. From bottom to top the line gets fuller, then $\mathbb{C}$ leaves the line.
intro.disguised: the way a number is written can fool you. Simplify it first, then find the lowest row that holds it.

build.natural: the primes, $1$ and the composites make up $\mathbb{N}$.

about.natural: $\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}$ is made of the primes $\mathbb{P}=\{2,3,5,7,\dots\}$, the number $1$ and the composites $\mathbb{K}=\{4,6,8,9,\dots\}$.
about.rational: $\mathbb{Q}$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ plus fractions such as $\tfrac12$ and $-\tfrac23$. Every rational number can be written as $\tfrac{m}{n}$ with $m,n\in\mathbb{Z}$, $n\neq 0$.
about.real: $\mathbb{R}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$ plus the irrational numbers $\mathbb{I}_r$, such as $\sqrt2$, $e$ and $\pi$. Its line is whole, with no gaps.
about.complex: $\mathbb{C}=\{a+bi\mid a,b\in\mathbb{R},\ i^2=-1\}$. A real number is a complex number with $b=0$, for example $3=3+0i$, so it sits on the line. What gets added: the numbers with $b\neq 0$, off the line.

reasons.one: $1$ is neither prime nor composite, so it has its own part of $\mathbb{N}$.
reasons.two: $2$ is divisible only by $1$ and $2$: a prime.
reasons.three: $3$ is divisible only by $1$ and $3$: a prime.
reasons.zero: $0$ is not a natural number. It first appears in $\mathbb{C}_a$.
reasons.negative: a negative integer, which first appears in $\mathbb{Z}$.
reasons.fraction: a fraction that is not an integer, which first appears in $\mathbb{Q}$.
reasons.sqrtTwo: $\sqrt2$ cannot be written as $\tfrac{m}{n}$: an irrational number. In the $\mathbb{Q}$ row its place is still a gap.
reasons.pi: $\pi=3.14159\dots$ has decimals that never stop and never repeat: an irrational number. In the $\mathbb{Q}$ row its place is still a gap.
reasons.imaginaryUnit: $i=0+1i$, so $a=0$ and $b=1$. Since $b\neq 0$, the point leaves the real line, $1$ unit up.
reasons.onePlusTwoI: $a=1$ and $b=2$: $1$ unit right, $2$ units up. Since $b\neq 0$, it is not a real number.
reasons.sixThirds: looks like a fraction, but $6\div 3=2$: a prime.
reasons.sqrtNine: has a root sign, but $3\times 3=9$, so $\sqrt9=3$: a prime.
reasons.minusEightQuarters: $-8\div 4=-2$: a negative integer, not a fraction.
reasons.iSquared: has an $i$, but $i^2=-1$ by definition: a negative integer.
reasons.threeQuarters: a terminating decimal: $0.75=\tfrac{75}{100}=\tfrac34$, so it is rational.
reasons.repeating: a repeating decimal is rational too: let $x=0.333\dots$, then $10x-x=3$, so $x=\tfrac13$.
reasons.sqrtEight: $\sqrt8=2\sqrt2$, and $\sqrt2$ is irrational, so $\sqrt8$ is irrational too.
reasons.sqrtMinusFour: no real number squares to $-4$. $\sqrt{-4}=2i$, because $(2i)^2=4i^2=-4$.

note.notBelow: but ${{value}}\notin {{set}}$, so it is not in any lower row.

complexNumbers.title: Complex Numbers

plot.intro: a complex number $z = a + bi$ is drawn as the point $(a, b)$: the real part $a$ on the horizontal axis $\mathrm{Re}(z)$, the imaginary part $b$ on the vertical axis $\mathrm{Im}(z)$.
plot.summary: every $z = a + bi$ has exactly one point $(a, b)$ in the plane, and every point has exactly one $z$.
plot.hint: click a point, or play to draw them one by one.
captions: $z_1 = 1 + 2i$: 1 to the right along $\mathrm{Re}(z)$, then 2 up. The point is $(1, 2)$.
$z_2 = -2 + i$: 2 to the left, then 1 up. The point is $(-2, 1)$.
$z_3 = -1 - 2i$: 1 to the left, then 2 down. The point is $(-1, -2)$.
$z_4 = 2 - i$: 2 to the right, then 1 down. The point is $(2, -1)$.

add.intro: real adds to real, imaginary to imaginary. In the plane: start at $z_1$, then walk as far as $z_2$.
add.summary: $z_1 + z_2 = 3 - i$. Adding means joining: the walk of $z_2$ (2 right, 3 down) is attached to the end of $z_1$.
add.hint: click a point, or play to add part by part.
captions: real part: $1 + 2 = 3$. From $z_1$ move 2 to the right.
imaginary part: $2 + (-3) = -1$. Move 3 down.

subtract.intro: real minus real, imaginary minus imaginary. In the plane: start at $z_1$, then walk as far as $z_2$ in the opposite direction.
subtract.summary: $z_1 - z_2 = -1 + 5i$. Subtracting $z_2$ is walking as far as $z_2$ the other way: 2 left, 3 up.
subtract.hint: click a point, or play to subtract part by part.
captions: real part: $1 - 2 = -1$. From $z_1$ move 2 to the left.
imaginary part: $2 - (-3) = 5$. Move 3 up.

multiply.intro: every term times every term, like $(a + b)(c + d)$. The difference: $i \cdot i = i^2 = -1$, so imaginary times imaginary moves to the real part.
multiply.summary: $z_1 \cdot z_2 = 8 + i$. The term $2i \cdot (-3i)$ looks imaginary, but $i^2 = -1$ makes it real: 6 to the right, not up.
multiply.hint: click a point, or play to fill the boxes one by one.
captions: $1 \cdot 2 = 2$, real. From 0 move 2 to the right.
$1 \cdot (-3i) = -3i$, imaginary. Move 3 down, right onto $z_2$, because $1 \cdot z_2 = z_2$.
$2i \cdot 2 = 4i$, imaginary. Move 4 up.
$2i \cdot (-3i) = -6i^2 = 6$, because $i^2 = -1$. So it is real: move 6 to the right.
real $2 + 6 = 8$, imaginary $-3i + 4i = i$. So $z_1 \cdot z_2 = 8 + i$.

divide.intro: multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate of the bottom, $\bar{z}_2$. The bottom becomes a real number, then each part is simply divided.
divide.hint: click a point, or play to divide step by step.
captions: conjugate of the bottom: $\bar{z}_2 = 2 + 3i$, the mirror of $z_2$ in the $\mathrm{Re}(z)$ axis.
bottom: $(2 - 3i)(2 + 3i) = 4 + 9 = 13$. The imaginary part cancels, so it is real.
divide by 13: $\tfrac{z_1}{z_2} = -\tfrac{4}{13} + \tfrac{7}{13}i$. Same direction as $-4 + 7i$, 13 times closer to 0.

conjugate.intro: the conjugate of $z = a + bi$ is $\bar{z} = a - bi$: the imaginary part changes sign. In the plane: a mirror in the $\mathrm{Re}(z)$ axis.
conjugate.summary: conjugate = mirror in the $\mathrm{Re}(z)$ axis. That is why $\overline{z_1 - z_2} = \bar{z}_1 - \bar{z}_2$: both are the point $(-1, -5)$.
conjugate.hint: click a point, or play to mirror them one by one.
captions: $\bar{z}_1 = 1 - 2i$: the mirror of $z_1$ in the $\mathrm{Re}(z)$ axis.
$\bar{z}_2 = 2 + 3i$: the mirror of $z_2$.
$z_1 - z_2 = -1 + 5i$, as on the $z_1 - z_2$ tab.
the mirror of $z_1 - z_2$ lands on the same point: $\overline{z_1 - z_2} = \bar{z}_1 - \bar{z}_2$.

extras.conjugateOfZ2: the mirror of $z_2$ in the $\mathrm{Re}(z)$ axis.
extras.numerator: this is the top, not yet divided by 13.
extras.quotient: it lies on the line from 0 to $-4 + 7i$, 13 times closer to 0.

complexNumbers.twoFormsFootnote: so $(1, 2)$ and $1 + 2i$ are the same number.
complexNumbers.whyIText: $x^2 + 1 = 0$ means $x^2 = -1$. The square of a real number is never negative, so $\mathbb{R}$ has no answer. With $i^2 = -1$, the answers are $x = i$ and $x = -i$.

productTags.footnote: rows from $z_1 = 1 + 2i$, columns from $z_2 = 2 - 3i$. Shaded boxes = real part.

a.reason: a declarative sentence, but "somewhat on" is neither true nor false: a bulb is either on or not on. It has no truth value, so it is not a proposition.

b.reason: a declarative sentence that is false, because $3 - 2 = 1$. A proposition with value F, written $Q$.

c.reason: a declarative sentence that is true. A proposition with value T, written $R$.

d.reason: a question, not a declarative sentence. So it is not a proposition.

e.reason: a suggestion, not a declarative sentence. So it is not a proposition.

f.text: The values of $x$ that satisfy $x^2 - 1 = 0$ are $x = 1$ and $x = -1$.
f.reason: a declarative sentence that is true: $1^2 - 1 = 0$ and $(-1)^2 - 1 = 0$. A proposition with value T, written $P$.

g.reason: a declarative sentence, but its value depends on $x$: $x = 1$ gives $2$ (prime), $x = 3$ gives $4$ (not prime). This is an open sentence, so it is not a proposition. A quantifier turns it into one: see the x + 1 prime tab.

captions.false: ({{letter}}) declarative, surely F: a proposition with value F, written ${{symbol}}$.

definition.rest: is a declarative sentence whose truth value is exactly one of true or false, and nothing else.

plusThree.reason: for any $x \in \mathbb{N}$, $x \ge 1$, so $x + 3 \ge 4$: always a natural number.
plusThree.step: all the examples here are true, but there are infinitely many other numbers in $\mathbb{N}$. A general reason is needed: {{reason}}

negationConjunctionDisjunction.title: Negation, Conjunction & Disjunction
negationConjunctionDisjunction.hint: click a row, or play to fill the table row by row.

readings: $P$ = T: it really is raining, so "it is not raining today" is false. The value flips: $\neg P$ = F.
$P$ = F: it is not raining, so "it is not raining today" is true. The value flips: $\neg P$ = T.
negation.definition: Let $P$ be a proposition. The negation of $P$ is not $P$, written $\neg P$. The negation of $P$ is false if $P$ is true, and true if $P$ is false.
reading: $\neg P$ is read "not $P$" or "the negation of $P$".
negation.intro: negation flips the truth value: T becomes F, F becomes T.

suppose: $P \wedge Q$: in good health *and* graduated from high school
readings: $P$ = T, $Q$ = T: graduated and in good health, like Amir. Both requirements are met, so $P \wedge Q$ = T: accepted.
$P$ = T, $Q$ = F: graduated but not in good health. One requirement fails, so $P \wedge Q$ = F: not accepted.
$P$ = F, $Q$ = T: in good health but did not graduate, like Ali. One requirement fails, so $P \wedge Q$ = F: not accepted.
$P$ = F, $Q$ = F: did not graduate and not in good health. Both requirements fail, so $P \wedge Q$ = F: not accepted.
conjunction.definition: Let $P$ and $Q$ be two propositions. The conjunction of $P$ and $Q$, written $P \wedge Q$, is true if both are true, and false otherwise.
reading: "but" is also a conjunction: "in good health but did not graduate".
conjunction.intro: a conjunction is T only when both are T.

suppose: $P \vee Q$: Amir goes to Bandung *or* Amad goes to Bandung
readings: $P$ = T, $Q$ = T: Amir and Amad both go to Bandung. "Or" here includes both, so $P \vee Q$ = T.
$P$ = T, $Q$ = F: only Amir goes. One true part is enough, so $P \vee Q$ = T.
$P$ = F, $Q$ = T: only Amad goes. One true part is enough, so $P \vee Q$ = T.
$P$ = F, $Q$ = F: nobody goes to Bandung. Both are false, so $P \vee Q$ = F.
disjunction.definition: Let $P$ and $Q$ be two propositions. The disjunction of $P$ and $Q$, written $P \vee Q$, is false if both are false, and true otherwise.
reading: "or" here includes both: $P \vee Q$ is still T when $P$ and $Q$ are both T.
disjunction.intro: a disjunction is F only when both are F.

sideBySide.footnote: $\wedge$ is T only in row 1, $\vee$ is F only in row 4.

enough.footnote: like the quantifiers: $\wedge$ is like $\forall$ (all must be T), $\vee$ is like $\exists$ (one T is enough).

examples.text: Amir did not pass the exam
examples.negation: Amir did not not pass the exam
examples.remark: the sentence already has "not"; its negation means Amir passed the exam.
$R$ is true, so $\neg R$ is false: row 1.

implicationBiconditional.title: Implication & Biconditional
implicationBiconditional.hint: click a row, or play to fill the table row by row.

suppose: $P \Rightarrow Q$: *if* Amir passes the exam, *then* his father throws a party
readings: $P$ = T, $Q$ = T: Amir passes and his father throws a party. The promise is kept, so $P \Rightarrow Q$ = T.
$P$ = T, $Q$ = F: Amir passes but his father throws no party. The promise is broken, so $P \Rightarrow Q$ = F. This is the only F row.
$P$ = F, $Q$ = T: Amir fails but his father throws a party anyway. The promise only covers Amir passing, so it is not broken: $P \Rightarrow Q$ = T.
$P$ = F, $Q$ = F: Amir fails and his father throws no party. The promise is not broken, so $P \Rightarrow Q$ = T.
implication.definition: Let $P$ and $Q$ be two propositions. The implication $P \Rightarrow Q$ is false if $P$ is true and $Q$ is false, and true otherwise.
reading: the order matters: $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $Q \Rightarrow P$ differ in rows 2 and 3.
implication.intro: an implication is F only when $P$ = T and $Q$ = F, otherwise T.

suppose: $P \Leftrightarrow Q$: I go to work *if and only if* I am healthy
readings: $P$ = T, $Q$ = T: I go to work and I am healthy. The values match, so $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ = T.
$P$ = T, $Q$ = F: I go to work while sick. The values differ, so $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ = F.
$P$ = F, $Q$ = T: I am healthy but stay home. The values differ, so $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ = F.
$P$ = F, $Q$ = F: I am sick and stay home. The values match, so $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ = T.
biconditional.definition: Let $P$ and $Q$ be two propositions. The biconditional of $P$ and $Q$, written $P \Leftrightarrow Q$, is true if both are true or both are false, and false otherwise.
reading: $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ is read "$P$ if and only if $Q$".
it holds two implications at once: if $P$ then $Q$, and if $Q$ then $P$.
biconditional.intro: a biconditional is T when $P$ and $Q$ are both T or both F.

implicationBiconditional.caption: row {{row}}: {{assign}}. {{reason}}, so ${{expression}}$ = {{result}}.

directions.footnote: $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ = T exactly in the rows where both directions are T: rows 1 and 4.

implication.false: $P$ must be T and $Q$ must be F

untested.body: The father's promise only talks about the case where Amir passes (rows 1 and 2). If Amir fails (rows 3 and 4), the promise says nothing: party or no party, the promise is not broken.

converse.sentence: $Q \Rightarrow P$: *if* I go to the doctor, *then* I am sick
converse.intro: the converse swaps $P$ and $Q$: $P \Rightarrow Q$ becomes $Q \Rightarrow P$.
converse.verdict: $Q \Rightarrow P$ and $P \Rightarrow Q$ differ in rows 2 and 3, so the converse does not always have the same value as the implication.

inverse.sentence: $\neg P \Rightarrow \neg Q$: *if* I am not sick, *then* I do not go to the doctor
inverse.intro: the inverse negates both and keeps the order: $P \Rightarrow Q$ becomes $\neg P \Rightarrow \neg Q$.
inverse.verdict: $\neg P \Rightarrow \neg Q$ and $P \Rightarrow Q$ differ in rows 2 and 3, so the inverse does not always have the same value as the implication.
reading: $\neg P \Rightarrow \neg Q$ is read "if not $P$ then not $Q$".
how to build it: negate $P$ and $Q$, keep their places.

contrapositive.sentence: $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$: *if* I do not go to the doctor, *then* I am not sick
contrapositive.intro: the contrapositive swaps and negates both: $P \Rightarrow Q$ becomes $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$.
contrapositive.verdict: $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$ and $P \Rightarrow Q$ match in all four rows: the contrapositive always has the same value as the implication.
reading: $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$ is read "if not $Q$ then not $P$".
how to build it: swap $P$ and $Q$, then negate both.

definition.intro: If $P \Rightarrow Q$ is an implication, then:
lines: (a) $Q \Rightarrow P$ is called the converse of $P \Rightarrow Q$;
(b) $\neg P \Rightarrow \neg Q$ is called the inverse of $P \Rightarrow Q$;
(c) $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$ is called the contrapositive of $P \Rightarrow Q$.

square.footnote: swap = swap the two propositions, negate = put $\neg$ on both. Forms at the two ends of the same diagonal always have the same value: the implication with the contrapositive, the converse with the inverse.

reading.same: left side {{left}}, right side {{right}}: the same.

cards.count: how many steps, how many rows?

order.footnote: a new column only uses columns that already exist, so the innermost part always comes first. All steps go in one table; there is no need for a separate table per part.

count.footnote: each letter can be T or F, so every new letter doubles the number of rows: $n$ letters, $2^n$ rows.

lookup.row: row {{row}} is enough, from the inside out:

Mother buys clothes *or* father does not buy a motorbike

lookup.footnote: when the value of every letter is known, the whole table is not needed: find the matching row, then work through its steps from the inside out.

definition.after: , written "$\equiv$", when all their truth values are the same.
definition.reading: $\equiv$ reads "is equivalent to", $\not\equiv$ reads "is not equivalent to".

series.footnote: like the quantifier $\forall$: every row has to match. One differing row is enough to say not equivalent.

items.negatedImplication: "$P$ but not $Q$" means the same as "it is not true that if $P$ then $Q$"
items.deMorgan: "it is not true that $P$ and $Q$" means the same as "not $P$ or not $Q$"
items.implicationAsDisjunction: "if $P$ then $Q$" means the same as "not $P$ or $Q$"
items.onlyQ: "$Q$" means the same as "if $P$ or not $Q$, then $Q$"
items.contrapositive: an implication and its contrapositive: "if $P$ then $Q$" means the same as "if not $Q$ then not $P$"
items.notDeMorgan: "it is not true that $P$ and $Q$" does not mean the same as "not $P$ and not $Q$"

pairs.footnote: values = the column from row 1 to row 4. The last line is not an equivalent pair: a common mistake when negating a conjunction.

legend.treeTrue: in the tree: T in the chosen row

rules.and: is T only when both are T
rules.or: is F only when both are F
rules.implies: is F only when the left part is T and the right part is F

verdict.tautology: check the last column: all {{value}}, so ${{expression}}$ is a tautology.
verdict.contradiction: check the last column: all {{value}}, so ${{expression}}$ is a contradiction.
verdict.neither: check the last column: not a tautology because rows {{falseRows}} are {{falseValue}}, not a contradiction because rows {{trueRows}} are {{trueValue}}.
verdict.valid: check the last column: all {{value}}. The implication is a tautology, so this argument is valid.
verdict.invalid: check the last column: row {{rows}} is {{value}}. The implication is not a tautology, so this argument is not valid. In that row every premise is true but the conclusion is false.

intro.tautology: Fill in the table step by step, then check the last column.
intro.argument: Join the premises with $\wedge$, then $\Rightarrow$ the conclusion. The argument is valid if that implication is a tautology.

formulas.implicationOrP: The last column decides: all T, all F, or mixed.

rain.reading: $P \wedge \neg P$: "it is raining today and it is not raining today"

modusPonens.label: modus ponens
modusPonens.title: modus ponens
premises: if the switch is on then the bulb is lit
modusPonens.intro: Premise 2 affirms the left part of premise 1.

modusTollens.label: modus tollens
modusTollens.title: modus tollens
premises: if the switch is on then the bulb is lit
modusTollens.intro: Premise 2 denies the right part of premise 1.

syllogism.label: syllogism
syllogism.title: syllogism
letters: I do not go to the beach
premises: if it is a holiday then I will go to the beach
if I go to the beach then I will swim
syllogism.conclusion: if it is a holiday then I will swim
syllogism.intro: The two implications meet at $Q$. There are three letters, so the table has 8 rows.

contrapositive.label: contrapositive
contrapositive.title: contrapositive
letters: I do not go to the doctor
premises: if I am sick then I go to the doctor
contrapositive.conclusion: if I do not go to the doctor then I am not sick
contrapositive.intro: Only one premise. The conclusion is its contrapositive.

meaningfulNotValid.label: sensible, not valid
meaningfulNotValid.title: the left turn argument
premises: if turning left then you may go on
meaningfulNotValid.intro: Looks like modus tollens, but premise 2 denies the left part of premise 1, not the right part.

wages go up

they do not pass the year

$x \neq 3$

if they go to the doctor then they get medicine
syllogism.conclusion: if they are sick then they get medicine

if $2^2$ is an integer then $2^4$ is an integer
syllogism.conclusion: if $2$ is an integer then $2^4$ is an integer

contrapositive.conclusion: if Jakarta does not flood then it does not rain

contrapositive.conclusion: if the people do not prosper then leaders are corrupt

reading.untested: a premise is false, so this row does not test the argument. The implication is {{value}} on its own.
reading.tested: every premise is true and the conclusion is true.
reading.counter: every premise is true but the conclusion is false: a counterexample. This one row is enough to say the argument is not valid.

cards.kinds: all T, all F, or mixed?

definition.tautology: A proposition is a **tautology** when it is always true, whatever the values of the propositions it is built from.
definition.contradiction: A compound proposition is a **contradiction** when it is always false, whatever the values of the propositions it is built from.

kindTable.name: called
kindTable.footnote: like the quantifier $\forall$: a tautology is T in every row. One F row is enough to say it is not a tautology, one T row is enough to say it is not a contradiction.

finals.name: called
finals.footnote: values = the last column from the first row to the last. Valid arguments are checked the same way: the implication must be a tautology.

argument.terms: The propositions given as reasons are the **premises**, the proposition drawn from them is the **conclusion**. Drawing a conclusion from premises is an **argument**.
argument.valid: An argument is **valid** when its premises are true and its conclusion is true as well.
argument.footnote: join the premises with $\wedge$, then $\Rightarrow$ the conclusion. If that implication is a tautology, the argument is valid.

lines: if Ani is pretty then Amir is handsome
Amir is not handsome
items.remark: it has the form of modus tollens, so it is valid. But Ani's looks have nothing to do with Amir's.

lines: if turning left then you may go on
not turning left
items.remark: it sounds reasonable at a crossing with traffic lights, but the implication is not a tautology.

meaning.footnote: logic checks whether an argument is valid, not whether it makes sense.

critical.counter: all premises true, conclusion false: a counterexample
critical.untested: a premise is F, so the implication is T on its own
critical.footnote: an implication is F only when its left part is T and its right part is F, that is, when every premise is true but the conclusion is false. So only the rows with all premises true need checking: if the conclusion is always T there, the argument is valid.

summary.name: name
summary.footnote: the last row is not a valid argument. It looks like modus tollens, but it denies the left part instead of the right part.
